blocks.text: It is not determined which language is meant by לשון כנען in Rashi and other writers of the Middle Ages. Sachs (Kerem Chemed vol. 7, p. 278), following Luzzatto, takes the יערוף לשון כנעני occurring in the Sifri (P. Haasinu) to be Syriac; this isolated example, however, cannot be decisive for all passages, cf. Fürst (L. Bl. d. Orients 1851, col. 10); thus in Natan's Aruch Greek is understood by this expression (see Landau: Marpe Laschon s.v. פרגין; cf. also Rashi on R. Haschana 13b and on this my contribution in Frankel's Monatsschrift etc. vol. 5, p. 478 s.v. פשאורו); thus further in Rashi on Deut. 3, 9 that expression means Icelandic, in which snow is still today called Snioor (cf. Mulder: Over de verdiensten van Raschi [Amsterdam 1826] p. 33). Landau (following Binjamin of Tudela, see the relevant citation in Rappoport in the treatise preceding the ער גל, p. 43) maintains that a Slavic language (Slavonic, Bohemian, Polish and Russian) is to be understood by it. — In any case Syriac cannot be meant in our passage, since the beetle is called ܟܝܟܡܐ [כיכמא] here too.
This word is missing in Landau's Marpe Laschon.

The sense of that proverb was expressed in two similar proverbs taken from the animal world. The one reads: גור טוב מכלב ביש לא תרבי גור ביש מכלב ביש על אחת כמה וכמה "Do not raise even a good-natured dog if it descends from an ill-natured bitch, and much less the bad pup of a bad bitch!" (Rabba Wajikra fol. 186, d); the other proverb is more pointed: מכלבא בישא גורא טבא לא נפיק "from a bad bitch no good-natured pup can descend" (Seder Olam ch. 25).

In the Jerusalem Talmud (Terumoth C. 8, fol. 45b) it says: it is permitted to eat, while they are inside the fruit, שקץ שבזיזין ובזבזין ובהגזין ובשקצים וברמשים; the word זבזין is probably corrupted from זבזבין.
Cyreniaci Achoren Deum invocant muscarum multitudine pestilentiam afferente, quae protinus intereunt, cum litatum est illi Deo.

The same was claimed of the larva of the ant-lion (Myrmeleo formicarius), that it had no anus at all, which however has now been refuted; it does have such an opening, but it seems not to discharge excrement, rather to process everything it consumes (Voigt l. c. 5, p. 307). The gnat too has an anus, only it perhaps may not live long enough to discharge its food again as excrement, which is what the Talmud may have meant.
They are called מויקי בית (Rabba Bereschit fol. 60, c).
Compare my contribution "Fabeln aus der Thierwelt" in the "Jüdisches Volksblatt" vol. 3, p. 116.
This last statement is repeated by all more recent zoologists; cf. e.g. Voigt l. c. 5, p. 223.
On מני see Winer: Bibl. Real-Wtb. 2, p. 244.
See on our passage specifically Tosephot on B. Kama 92b s.v. שיתין and in general Tos. on M. Katan 28a s.v. שיתין.
Fleas, gnats and flies are also called: enemies of man (Jalk. Schim. part 2, fol. 139, d); see also p. 85, note ***.

He belongs to those חיין אינם חיים, whose life does not deserve to be called life, since the biting and itching do not let them take joy in life; the refined wickedness of slave traders, who torment the unfortunate beings during transport by ship through uncleanliness, such as scabies and lice, so that they are induced to think only of their momentary physical sufferings, is well known.

The itch mite (Acarus scabici; Voigt l. c. 4, p. 181) is not meant here, since it is the consequence, not the cause, of scabies; Brecher (das Transcendentale etc. p. 171) therefore need not be in doubt about this.

Perhaps in Sabbat 107b one is to understand by טיפויי the dead nits, and by ביצי כינים the living ones. — The following words of Aristotle (Thierg. 5, 1, 5) may find a place here; they read: "The animals that arise spontaneously on animals, plants, or their parts undeniably have separate sexes, and they also produce something through their copulation, but never a creature of their own kind, rather something imperfect, as e.g. from lice the nits, and from flies and butterflies the egg-like worms, from which neither a creature like their parents (?) nor any other animal emerges, but which only remain what they are." — Of the nits it is indeed true that they remain in their state and do not develop into an articulated insect.

The poet Juda b. Salomo al-Charisi (in his Tachkemoni P. 50) jests aptly about the flea; he says: "Wretched flea, surly guest of my bed, who prepares delight for yourself with the plunder of my blood, creates for yourself the highest feast, to spoil my feasts and Sabbaths for me —; and yet my wise friends said: By all means leave the insolent robber unmolested on the Sabbath! Really? But no! They also said: 'Whoever wants to kill you, kill him first!'"

In the Jerusalem Talmud it says: the bedbug serves against leeches (cf. Appendix s.v. שכלון); compare with this Harduin (in the notes and emendations to Plin. h. n. 29, sect. 17), who reports from Marcellus Empiricus: Ad eos, qui sanguisugas inscii devorant, cimicum in carbonibus positorum fumus remedium est: si ore hianti, et faucibus apertis excipiantur, ejici enim et expelli devoratas sanguisugas hac ratione certissimum est. It follows from this at the same time that leeches have a sense of smell.
פשפש may well be read with ש, from פשה to multiply, since this vermin multiplies greatly; see however Levita (Tischbi s.v. פשפש), who derives it from "to search": man searches out the insect.
